$comment: The LaunchDarkly resources this repo expects, as data. `npm run seed` reads this
file plus seed/snippets/, validates the pair, and prints exactly what must exist
in LaunchDarkly. It does not mutate LaunchDarkly: creating these resources is a
human-gated step you drive from the dashboard or the .claude/commands/factory-*
slash commands over the LaunchDarkly MCP server, which authenticates with OAuth
and needs no write-scoped API token checked into a public repo.
/factory-bootstrap creates this whole list once so a tutorial reader can
start at Play. Later changes still go through /factory-classify and a human.
Two axes, and keeping them apart is what makes a guarded rollout mean anything:
Axis A — WHICH groove. One variation per groove, selected by TARGETING.
This is arrangement. It changes several times a minute.
Axis B — WHICH VERSION of a groove's text. Selected by ROLLOUT. This is the
thing you guard. To test a change to four-on-the-floor you create
snippet #2, create a NEW variation pinning it, and roll that out
against the original on the rule that already serves it.
Variation count is grooves + candidates, never grooves x versions.
$model: Every variation is created with the same model. Note the shape — the two
fields are NOT interchangeable and the API rejects the obvious guess:
modelConfigKey carries the dated id, modelName does not.
A variation's parameters MUST include gain_ceiling. A variation without one
silently disables the guardrail for everyone it is served to, because
lintPattern skips the gain check rather than failing closed.

contextKinds.name: Musician
contextKinds.description: Which agent is generating — drummer, bassist, or keys.

contextKinds.name: Performance
contextKinds.description: The conductor's state at generation time: section, energy, whether this is a section boundary.

contextKinds.name: Listener
contextKinds.description: Who is listening — the audience dimension that selects a shelf of vocabulary.

contextKinds.name: Request
contextKinds.description: One generation. THE RANDOMIZATION UNIT for guarded rollouts, and the analysis unit on both guardrail metrics. Built-in kind: the docs recommend it for backend-only changes, and every autogenerated AI metric already suggests it.

metrics.name: Peak gain
metrics.description: The loudest gain value in the published pattern, computed from the pattern string with no audio. Numeric value metric, lower is better.

metrics.name: Ceiling breach rate
metrics.description: Did this generation ask for more gain than the musician's stated ceiling. THE ROLLOUT GUARDRAIL. Binary conversion, lower is better. This is a POLICY metric — it measures whether the output obeyed a documented invariant, not whether it sounded good. That is a stronger claim, and it is true.

metrics.name: Publish success rate
metrics.description: Did this generation reach the speakers at all. The guardrail for the strict-mix-gate CODE change: a gate that is too strict does not sound bad, it makes the band freeze — nothing new arrives. Higher is better.

flags.name: Strict mix gate
flags.description: When true, the validator uses strict_gain_ceiling instead of gain_ceiling. The code-change unit of the tutorial. Create it serving false, then turn the flag ON so targeting applies. Do not start a rollout here.

$strictNote: 0.6, not 0.95. Measured: at 0.95 the model simply complies on retry and
squeezes the kick down to exactly 0.95, so 39 of 44 generations still
published — a stutter, not a freeze. At 0.6 it cannot comply without
abandoning the kick range of 1.0-1.15 stated in drummer-mix-discipline,
which is where the ceiling and the ratchet both live, so both attempts
fail and hold-last-known-good takes over: 28 generations, 0 published,
28 held. That is the point of the chapter — a gate that is too strict
does not sound bad, it makes the band stop evolving.

$comment: First match wins. These rules encode the judgment that commit 1012e45 put
into the selection prompt: a moment fires ONLY at a real boundary, and it
matches the section being ENTERED, never the one coming later. A boundary
into a LOW-energy section deliberately has no rule — it falls through to a
groove, which is the model abstaining, made deterministic.
The lounge rules come first because the lounge shelf is thin: swing-feel is
its only groove and fill-transition its only moment. Without an explicit
lounge-boundary rule, a lounge listener at a high-energy boundary would be
served build-up — peak-hour vocabulary that is not on their shelf.
Deterministic targeting costs variety: #chooseSkills used to let the model
switch grooves mid-section, and a 64-cycle loop gets repetitive without it.
A percentage rollout ACROSS groove variations inside one rule restores the
stochasticity — and it is the same mechanism as the guarded rollout, which
makes 'the rollout dial is the arrangement dial' concrete rather than clever.

$ceilingNote: 0.9, not 0.85. The sub-drop vocabulary lands exactly on 0.9 and states that
limit in its own text, so a 0.85 ceiling would make the bassist reject every
sub-drop and hold — the band would lose its moments on day one. The
deterministic guardrail found an inconsistency the vibe check had missed;
reconciling it BEFORE enabling the check is the difference between a good
tutorial beat and a broken demo.

$comment: The lounge rule is unconditional and comes first BECAUSE the lounge bassist
has no moment at all — walking-bass is the whole shelf. This is the real
fallthrough the thin shelf needs; without it a lounge boundary serves
sub-drop, which is peak-hour vocabulary.
